name: Damon self-ligating braces

angle.text: Forum users rate Damon braces highly and credit them with arch expansion, even jaw or maxilla changes. They are marketed for low friction and non-extraction treatment; reviews find mostly mixed benefits, and jaw-forward claims are unproven.

summary: Passive self-ligating braces sold on low friction and arch expansion; forums rate them top, reviews find mostly mixed benefits.
note: No trials show facial-bone change from the bracket type.
currentQuick:
Damon braces hold the wire with a sliding door instead of rubber ties. They are marketed for lower friction, lighter forces and arch expansion.
Looksmax forums often call them the best braces for smile and arch width, but systematic reviews summarised on Wikipedia find only some benefits, chiefly lower friction and shorter chair time.
How it works: A passive clip lets the archwire slide with little pressure, so teeth move under light forces as the wire shape guides alignment.
Risks and caveats: Risks are those of braces generally. Reviews do not link the bracket type to extra hygiene problems or benefits; claims of jaw changes are unstudied.
deepLead:
Damon braces are a line of self-ligating orthodontic brackets, which hold the archwire with a built-in sliding door instead of elastic ties. The Damon SL1 was introduced in 1996 and is classed as a passive self-ligating system. Manufacturers and some orthodontists say the design reduces friction and allows lighter forces, and the system is often marketed for arch expansion without extractions.
On looksmax.org, Damon braces are discussed as a way to widen the dental arch, improve the smile and, according to some posters, support jaw development. Published reviews describe a more modest picture: friction is the most consistently reported advantage in laboratory conditions, while claims about faster treatment, comfort and hygiene are mixed or unsupported.

name: Teeth whitening pens

angle.text: Users reach for whitening pens as a portable, at-home way to brighten their smile between other treatments. Evidence on pens specifically comes from laboratory studies.

summary: Brush-on gel pens for at-home whitening; evidence on pens specifically is lab-only.
note: Peroxide limits differ by region; sensitivity and gum irritation reported with peroxide whiteners.
currentQuick:
Whitening pens are brush-on gel applicators for at-home tooth whitening, a convenient alternative to strips or trays.
Research specific to pens consists of in vitro studies of peroxide penetration, enamel effects and filling colour; no human trials of pens were found.
How it works: The gel, often peroxide-based, breaks down stain molecules on and in enamel when applied to the tooth surface.
Risks and caveats: Peroxide products can cause tooth sensitivity and gum irritation, and may affect enamel texture and tooth-coloured fillings. Allowed peroxide strengths differ between the EU and US.
deepLead:
Teeth whitening pens are over-the-counter applicator pens that brush a peroxide-based or other whitening gel onto the tooth surface. They are one of several at-home options, alongside strips, trays, rinses and whitening toothpastes. The general Wikipedia article on tooth whitening does not mention pens specifically, so most of what is known comes from small laboratory studies.
In vitro work has examined how much hydrogen peroxide from pen and varnish products reaches the pulp chamber, how the products affect enamel, and how they act on tooth-coloured fillings. Regulation of peroxide strength differs by region: in the EU retail products may contain up to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide, while the US FDA endorses gels below 6 percent hydrogen peroxide or up to 16 percent carbamide peroxide.

name: Peroxycarboxylic (PAP) whitening

angle.text: PAP is promoted as a peroxide-free whitening agent for people who want lighter teeth with less sensitivity. The support is one small laser-activated study.

summary: Peroxide-free whitening agent (PAP) with one small laser-activated study behind it.
note: Published human evidence is a single 15-patient study.
currentQuick:
PAP is a non-peroxide whitening agent sold in some whitening products as an alternative to hydrogen peroxide.
Only a small 2025 study of fifteen patients with laser activation was found, so the evidence is thin.
How it works: A peroxycarboxylic acid is applied to teeth to oxidise stain compounds, optionally activated by light or laser.
Risks and caveats: Safety and sensitivity data are limited to that small study; no long-term data were found.
deepLead:
PAP whitening uses phthalimidoperoxycaproic acid, a peroxycarboxylic acid marketed as a non-peroxide-based tooth whitening agent. It is promoted as an alternative to hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide products, which are associated with tooth sensitivity.
Published evidence is sparse. A 2025 small study evaluated PAP activated by an 810-nm diode laser in fifteen patients with mild to moderate stains. This article is correspondingly short.

name: VITA shade guide

chain: Tabs A1 to D4 rate tooth color
angle.text: Dentists and whitening-focused users use the VITA scale to put a number on how light teeth are before and after treatment. It is a measurement reference rather than a treatment, and is widely used in cosmetic dentistry.

summary: The A1-D4 tooth-colour scale dentists use to describe and track whitening results.
note: A measuring scale, not a treatment; visual matching accuracy varies.
currentQuick:
The VITA shade guide is a set of tooth-coloured tabs used to name how light or dark teeth are, from A1 to D4.
It is a measurement reference, so it is used in studies and in forum talk to record whitening progress.
How it works: A clinician holds tabs next to the tooth and picks the closest match by value and chroma; instruments can also measure colour.
Risks and caveats: It carries no risk itself. Studies report coverage gaps in shade guides and differences between visual and instrument readings.
deepLead:
The VITA classical shade guide is a set of tooth-coloured tabs, labelled A1 to D4, used by dentists to describe and match tooth colour. It is arranged by value (lightness) and chroma (colour intensity). In whitening and cosmetic dentistry it serves as a reference scale for stating how light teeth are before and after treatment.
Studies in dental research have examined its limitations, including colour coverage errors and the accuracy of visual shade matching compared with instruments. In appearance communities, shade numbers are used as shorthand for how white teeth are.

name: Temporal brow lift

angle.text: Patients and looksmaxxing communities seek it to lift a drooping brow tail and open up the eye area, grouping it with eye-area surgery. The lift is visible after surgery and is documented in surgical series, with debate over technique.

summary: Surgical lateral eyebrow lift through temple incisions; documented in surgical series, with surgeon debate over technique.
note: Frontal branch facial nerve is the structure at risk; recurrence reported with some methods.
currentQuick:
A temporal brow lift raises the outer eyebrow through hidden incisions at the temples, sometimes with an endoscope.
Evidence is mostly surgical case series and technique comparisons; there are no large randomised trials among the sources used.
How it works: Tissue at the brow tail is released and re-fixed higher at the temple, by subcutaneous, endoscopic or combined methods.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include nerve injury, numbness, hair loss, infection, bleeding and recurrence of brow drop.
deepLead:
A temporal (lateral) brow lift is a surgical procedure that raises the outer part of the eyebrow using incisions placed in the hair-bearing temple area. It is one of several brow-lifting approaches that also include coronal, endoscopic, direct and internal (transblepharoplasty) lifts. Patients seek it to lift a drooping brow tail and open the eye area; looksmaxxing communities group it with eye-area surgery.
Studies describe subcutaneous and endoscopic temporal variants, various fixation techniques and results in case series. Evidence is mainly surgical case series and comparative studies, and surgeons disagree about the best approach.

name: Cheek lift

angle.text: Cheek lifts are used in facial rejuvenation to raise midface tissue, and some young men discuss them for a more defined look. The studies concern aging faces; claims for young men are untested.

summary: Surgical repositioning of sagging cheek tissue, studied mainly in ageing faces; looksmaxxing talk about it for young men is largely untested.
note: Evidence is mostly surgeon-reported technique series; surgical risks include nerve injury, haematoma and eyelid complications.
currentQuick:
A cheek lift, or midface lift, moves sagging cheek tissue and fat upward. Most published descriptions come from surgeons treating ageing faces, often alongside eyelid surgery or a facelift.
On looksmax.org it is mentioned by men who think their cheeks look flat or hollow and wonder how much it would change their appearance. There is little published evidence on that use.
How it works: Surgeons lift the cheek soft tissue, sometimes beneath the periosteum, through incisions at the lower eyelid, hairline or inside the mouth, and fix it in a higher position. Non-surgical options such as threads, fillers and ultrasound devices are used for milder cases.
Risks and caveats: General facelift references list haematoma, nerve injury, scarring and eyelid malposition among possible complications; smoking raises the risk of skin necrosis. Surgical cheek-lift results are documented mainly in surgeon-authored series rather than controlled trials.
deepLead:
A cheek lift, also called a midface lift, is a cosmetic surgical procedure that repositions sagging soft tissue of the cheek, including the malar fat pad, to a higher position on the face. It is performed under the broader heading of facial rejuvenation and is often combined with eyelid surgery or a full facelift .
Surgical descriptions in the literature include approaches through the lower eyelid, through the mouth and hairline, and by endoscope, with some techniques working beneath the periosteum, the membrane covering the facial bones . Non-surgical alternatives that are marketed for lifting the cheeks, such as threads, fillers and energy-based devices, are discussed separately from surgical cheek lifts .
In looksmaxxing communities the procedure is discussed mainly by younger men who report a hollow or aged look in the midface and ask how much a cheek lift would improve their appearance. Published evidence on the procedure is largely surgeon-authored technique descriptions rather than controlled trials.

name: Facial feminization surgery

chain: Brow, nose, cheek and jaw reshaped
angle.text: Developed for transgender women, FFS is now eyed by some looksmaxxers for brow bone, nose and cheek work to improve facial harmony. The surgical changes are visible; use for male faces is discussed in forums.

summary: A set of bone and soft-tissue facial operations developed for transgender women, now eyed by some looksmaxxers for brow, nose and cheek work.
note: Evidence is from transgender patient cohorts; use for appearance goals in cisgender men is untested.
currentQuick:
Facial feminization surgery is a group of operations that soften masculine facial features: lowering the hairline, shaving the brow ridge, reshaping the nose, building up cheeks, and reducing the chin, jaw and Adam's apple.
It was developed in the 1980s by Douglas Ousterhout for transgender women. Reviews report improved quality of life and a low complication rate, though the studies are mostly case series. On looksmax.org, a few users discuss borrowing its techniques for male faces.
How it works: Surgeons plan from CT and MRI imaging and then reshape bone (brow ridge, chin, jaw), soft tissue (nose, lips, brows), and add volume to cheeks with implants or fat. Operations are large and may be staged or combined.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include nerve injury, infection, implant displacement, fat resorption, bone-healing problems after forehead work, and vocal changes after tracheal shave. These are major operations under general anaesthesia and costs can be high; coverage depends on country and insurer.
deepLead:
Facial feminization surgery (FFS) is an umbrella term for reconstructive procedures that alter typically masculine facial features toward more typically feminine ones. It is performed mostly for transgender women and other transfeminine people, and includes work on the hairline, forehead and brow ridge, nose, cheeks, lips, chin and jaw, and the thyroid cartilage (Adam's apple) .
Its techniques derive from maxillofacial, ear-nose-throat and plastic and reconstructive surgery. Surgeon Douglas Ousterhout is credited with pioneering most of the procedures beginning in the early 1980s . Systematic reviews describe improved well-being and quality of life after FFS with a low complication rate, while noting that the evidence base is mostly case series .
In looksmaxxing communities, FFS is discussed in a different framing: some users on looksmax.org consider borrowing its brow, nose and cheek techniques to alter forehead, eye area and facial width in men .

name: Zygomatic reduction

angle.text: People with a wide or prominent midface seek cheekbone reduction, popular in Asian aesthetic surgery, for a narrower face. The change is visible after healing; the wiki's sources contain no outcome studies.

summary: Surgery to narrow or flatten the cheekbones; popular in Asian aesthetic surgery, with no outcome studies in the wiki's sources.
note: Forum members themselves report mixed before-and-after outcomes; no studies found.
currentQuick:
Zygomatic reduction is a surgery that reshapes or repositions the cheekbones to make the face narrower. It is also called malarplasty or cheekbone shaving.
On looksmax.org, users with wide faces discuss it and argue over whether it helps or ruins proportions. No studies were found for this wiki entry.
How it works: The bone of the cheek is cut and reshaped or repositioned inward, as forum posters describe it. Some say shaving mainly reduces forward projection rather than width.
Risks and caveats: Forum users describe results ranging from very good to very bad. It is a bone-cutting operation under anaesthesia; no complication data were available in the sources used here.
deepLead:
Zygomatic reduction, also called malarplasty, cheekbone reduction or cheekbone shaving, is a surgical procedure intended to narrow or lower the projection of the cheekbones (the zygomatic bones). The zygomatic bone forms the cheekbone and part of the eye socket wall .
The procedure is discussed in looksmaxxing forums mainly by people with wide faces, with participants disagreeing about whether width comes from bone or fat and whether the surgery improves or harms facial proportions . The material available for this entry is limited to a general anatomy reference and forum discussion.

name: Serdev suture

angle.text: Users consider Serdev suture lifting as a minimally invasive option within the thread-lift family for lifting facial tissue. The lift is visible when placed; published evidence on this specific technique is thin.

summary: A needle-suture thread lifting method from the suspension-thread family, with thin published evidence on the specific technique.
note: Early sutures increased inflammatory reaction; threads can be hard to remove.
currentQuick:
The Serdev suture is a thread-lift technique in which sutures are placed under the skin to hold sagging tissue up, rather than cutting out skin. It is associated with a surgeon named Serdev.
The sources available are thin: a general review of suspension threads and a general encyclopedia entry on thread lifts. No studies specific to the Serdev technique were found.
How it works: The sources describe suture threads placed in the dermis and subcutis to lift lax tissue; they do not detail the Serdev needle method.
Risks and caveats: A 2016 review reports that early sutures increased inflammatory reaction. A general reference notes that threads can be difficult to remove and that practitioner training varies.
deepLead:
The Serdev suture is a needle-based suture lifting technique for facial rejuvenation, associated with a surgeon named Serdev, who introduced a polycaproamide suture for facial lifting. It belongs to the broader family of suspension or thread lifts .
A 2016 review of suspension threads states that Sulamanidze and colleagues began using polypropylene threads after Serdev introduced a suture made of polycaproamide, and that these early sutures increased inflammatory reaction . Thread lifts are described in general references as non-surgical alternatives to facelifts, with some safety concerns about variable practitioner training .

name: Facial Autologous Muscular Injection (FAMI)

chain: Own fat injected into facial muscle
angle.text: Aesthetic clinics use FAMI, a fat-grafting variant, to restore volume and contour in the face with the patient's own fat. It appears alongside lipostructure in a 2007 review, and little is published on it specifically.

summary: A fat-grafting variant that places a patient's own fat into facial muscle; almost nothing is published on it specifically.
note: Evidence specific to FAMI is limited to a single review mention.
currentQuick:
FAMI is a facial fat-grafting approach in which a person's own fat is injected into facial muscle. A 2007 review lists it among newer methods meant to rejuvenate the whole face in three dimensions.
The wiki's sources contain little else on it, so this entry is short.
How it works: Fat is harvested from elsewhere on the body and injected into facial muscle, as the name describes. The sources give no further technical detail.
Risks and caveats: General fat grafting references list swelling, bruising, haematoma, contour irregularities, infection and partial reabsorption of the fat. FAMI-specific safety data were not found.
deepLead:
Facial Autologous Muscular Injection (FAMI), also written as fat autograft muscle injection, is a facial fat-grafting technique in which the patient's own fat is injected into facial muscle for volume restoration and contouring. A 2007 review of fat transfer lists it with lipostructure and facial fat rebalancing as newer concepts aimed at three-dimensional rejuvenation of the whole face .
The same review states that practical means of objectively measuring fat-transfer outcomes are lacking . Wikipedia mentions FAMI only in a notice proposing to merge a separate FAMI article into its fat grafting article, and does not describe the technique . Evidence specific to FAMI is very limited.

name: BaByliss trimmers/stylers

chain: Sharp, even hair and beard lines
angle.text: Users reach for BaByliss clippers and trimmers to keep haircuts, fades, beard edges and neckline tidy at home, and the sharper lines are visible immediately. It is one of several professional-style grooming tool brands; no appearance-outcome studies exist for the brand.

summary: A French-origin, Conair-owned brand of clippers, trimmers and hot tools; grooming gear with no appearance-outcome studies.
note: No product tests or community material were available for this entry.
currentQuick:
BaByliss makes hair dryers, straighteners, curling irons, clippers and beard trimmers. The brand began in France in 1960 and has been owned by Conair since 1995.
This entry is short because the available sources cover the company and general clipper design rather than specific products.
How it works: Clippers and trimmers cut hair with two close-fitting blades, one moving sideways against the other, driven by a motor.
Risks and caveats: No safety data on specific models were available. A general reference notes blades need lubrication and that ceramic blades can break.
deepLead:
BaByliss is a French personal care brand, now owned by the American group Conair, that sells hair dryers, curling irons, straighteners and, under its professional and men's lines, hair clippers and beard trimmers . Within grooming discussions, its trimmers and stylers are one of several professional-style tool brands.
The sources available for this entry cover the company's history and general clipper technology; no published tests of BaByliss products or forum discussion were available.

name: Remington IPL home device

angle.text: Users run the Remington iLight at home to thin out body or facial hair over repeated sessions as an alternative to shaving or clinic treatment. Home IPL as a category has been studied on light-to-medium skin; trials of this specific device are not found.

summary: Remington's home IPL flasher: reduces hair over repeated sessions on light-to-medium skin, no device-specific trials.
note: Manufacturer limits use to light-to-medium skin tones.
currentQuick:
A consumer IPL device that flashes broad-spectrum light to damage hair follicles over multiple sessions.
Evidence for IPL exists for clinic systems; none was found for this specific device.
How it works: Melanin in the hair absorbs the light and heats the follicle; only growing hairs respond, so sessions are repeated.
Risks and caveats: Burns, redness and pigment changes are reported with light-based removal; the manufacturer limits use to lighter skin tones.
deepLead:
Remington sells home intense pulsed light (IPL) hair-removal devices under its iLight line. IPL uses broad-spectrum light absorbed by melanin in the hair to heat and damage the follicle, and repeated sessions are needed because only follicles in the growth phase respond.
Wikipedia cites Remington as stating that IPL and laser devices should be used only on light to medium skin tones and work best on darker hair; the article presents this as a manufacturer claim. Remington Products itself is an American personal-care brand whose history runs from 1937 electric shavers to current ownership by Spectrum Brands.
No clinical trials of this specific device were found.

name: Veet depilatory cream

chain: Hair wiped off at skin surface
angle.text: Users apply Veet to leave arms, legs, chest or other areas smooth within minutes, without a razor. The smooth result is visible immediately and hair typically regrows within days; the effect is a cosmetic removal rather than a studied treatment.

summary: Chemical hair-dissolving cream from Reckitt: fast, painless-at-the-surface hair removal that regrows in days.
note: Alkaline thioglycolate chemistry can irritate skin; patch-test guidance appears on labels.
currentQuick:
Veet is a mass-market depilatory brand. Its creams dissolve the hair shaft chemically so hair can be wiped away at the skin surface, as an alternative to shaving or waxing.
Hair regrows because the follicle is not affected, and no clinical trials of the creams were found.
How it works: Thioglycolate salts in a high-pH base break the disulfide bonds in hair keratin, softening the shaft until it can be wiped off.
Risks and caveats: Irritation and chemical burns are possible with alkaline depilatories; a 2002 case series linked Veet wax strips (not creams) to allergic contact dermatitis. Labels advise patch testing.
deepLead:
Veet is a brand of chemical depilatory products, mainly creams, lotions and gels, that remove body hair by dissolving the keratin of the hair shaft so it can be wiped off at the skin surface. It is owned by Reckitt Benckiser and traces its origin to a Canadian product sold under the name Neet from 1919.
The active chemistry is the same family used across the depilatory category: thioglycolate salts in an alkaline base that break the disulfide bonds in keratin. Because the hair is cut below the skin surface but the follicle is left intact, hair regrows; Wikipedia notes depilatories do not destroy the dermal papilla.
No clinical trials of Veet creams for appearance outcomes are indexed. The published literature on the brand consists mainly of a dermatology report of allergic contact dermatitis linked to Veet wax-strip products, which are a different product type from the creams.

name: Nair depilatory

chain: Hair wiped away at the surface
angle.text: Nair is a long-standing drugstore way to remove body hair quickly without shaving, and the smooth result is visible straight away. Users commonly repeat it every few days as hair regrows.

summary: Classic drugstore depilatory cream: dissolves hair at the surface, regrows in days, irritation is the main caveat.
note: Alkaline chemistry; labels advise patch testing.
currentQuick:
Nair is a long-running chemical hair remover, launched in 1940 and now owned by Church & Dwight. It is sold in women's and men's lines.
It is a temporary method: the follicle is left intact so hair grows back.
How it works: Thioglycolate or calcium hydroxide breaks keratin's disulfide bonds so the hair can be wiped off.
Risks and caveats: Harsh actives can irritate skin; no brand-specific clinical studies were found.
deepLead:
Nair is an American brand of chemical depilatory products, including creams, lotions and sprays, that remove hair by breaking down keratin so it can be wiped from the skin. According to Wikipedia, the original lotion launched in 1940 and the brand is now owned by Church & Dwight, which bought it from Carter-Wallace in 2001.
The name is described as a portmanteau of "no hair." Its depilatories use calcium hydroxide and, in some formulas, potassium thioglycolate to break the disulfide bonds in hair keratin, with softening agents such as mineral oil added to offset the harshness of the actives. The depilatory category in general leaves the dermal papilla intact, so hair regrows.
No clinical studies specific to the brand were found.

name: Manscaped trimmers

angle.text: Manscaped sells trimmers marketed for men's body and below-the-belt grooming, letting users shorten and tidy hair without fully removing it. The trimmed result is visible immediately; the brand is discussed mostly for marketing and price rather than any studied outcome.

summary: Heavily marketed men's body-grooming trimmer brand; criticised for premium pricing.
note: Reviews cited by Grokipedia raise pricing and trim-guard durability concerns.
currentQuick:
Manscaped sells electric trimmers aimed at male body and pubic grooming, with a strongly humorous direct-to-consumer brand.
Trimming is cosmetic and temporary; no clinical studies were found.
How it works: Rotary or foil blades cut hair at skin level, with guards for length.
Risks and caveats: Nicks or irritation are generally possible; critics cite price and guard durability.
deepLead:
Manscaped is a San Diego direct-to-consumer brand of men's grooming tools, founded in 2016 by Paul Tran and Steve King, best known for the Lawn Mower electric trimmer for body and pubic hair.
The brand built its profile on humour-driven advertising and the term "manscaping." Wikipedia records a 2018 Shark Tank appearance, a 2020 campaign with Rob Gronkowski, and a terminated 2021 SPAC merger at about a $1 billion valuation. Grokipedia reports 2020 sales of $65 million, and criticism of pricing and trim-guard durability.
No clinical studies of the trimmers were found.

name: Electric tweezers

chain: Fewer regrowing hairs, cleaner brows or skin
angle.text: Users pick electric tweezers to pluck brows, facial and stray body hair, with some versions sold on the idea that an electrical pulse damages the root so hair stays away longer. That regrowth claim has no human studies behind it.

summary: Battery-powered pluckers, some sold with a claim of damaging the root; no human studies found.
note: Efficacy and safety claims for the electrified type are untested in the sources found.
currentQuick:
Electric tweezers are powered tweezers sold for plucking hair; some are described as sending an electrical signal to the root.
No clinical evidence was found.
How it works: Motorised grip, or an electrical signal at the tip intended to damage the root.
Risks and caveats: No safety data were found; skin irritation is a general plucking risk.
deepLead:
Electric tweezers is a name used for two different things: powered tweezers (a motor-driven gripping tool, covered by patents such as a 2006 filing for a motorised tweezer) and, in hair removal, tweezers that pass an electrical signal through the tip to damage the hair root so it does not regrow. Wikipedia describes the latter as an intended method of depilation.
The term also appears in physics, where "electric tweezers" use electric fields to manipulate nanoparticles, which is unrelated to appearance.
No clinical studies of electric tweezers for hair removal were found.

name: Braun Silk-expert IPL

angle.text: Users choose Braun Silk-expert IPL for at-home hair reduction, with versions using a skin-tone sensor to adjust or block flashes. Home IPL as a category has trial support for hair reduction; trials specific to this line are not found.

summary: Braun's home IPL with a skin-tone sensor: sensor-limited safety, no device-specific trials found.
note: Light-based removal is limited by skin tone and hair colour.
currentQuick:
A home IPL hair-removal device from Braun, described as having a skin-tone sensor.
Sources found cover IPL in general rather than this product.
How it works: Pulsed light is absorbed by hair melanin, heating the follicle; multiple sessions are needed.
Risks and caveats: Burns, redness and pigmentation changes are reported with IPL; manufacturers restrict use to lighter skin tones.
deepLead:
Braun Silk-expert is Braun's home intense pulsed light (IPL) hair-removal line, with versions described as having a skin-tone sensor. Braun is a Procter & Gamble subsidiary, and Wikipedia lists IPL appliances and epilators among its beauty-care products.
IPL heats hair follicles through melanin absorption and requires repeated sessions. Wikipedia cites manufacturer statements that such devices suit light to medium skin tones and work best on darker hair.
No device-specific clinical studies or detailed product sources were found, so this entry is brief.

name: Philips Lumea

angle.text: The Philips Lumea is a handheld IPL device used at home for long-term hair reduction on the body and face as an alternative to clinic treatment. Home IPL has some trial support for hair reduction, while evidence for this particular model is limited.

summary: Philips home IPL hair-removal device; the category has some trial support for hair reduction, but evidence specific to this model is thin.
note: Home IPL is generally described as suited to darker hair on lighter skin tones.
currentQuick:
The Philips Lumea is a consumer handheld device that uses intense pulsed light (IPL) for hair removal at home. It belongs to a category of home devices marketed as an alternative to salon or clinic treatment.
This article is short because the sources available describe the IPL category rather than this specific model. Clinical IPL generally reduces hair growth over repeated sessions, and encyclopedic sources describe it as typically less effective than laser.
How it works: IPL flashes broad-spectrum light that is absorbed by melanin in the hair, heating and damaging the follicle. Only hairs in the growth phase respond, so treatments are repeated over weeks.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks of IPL include hyperpigmentation and eye injury if misused; a review of home IPL safety discussed the need for eye safety in consumer designs. Light, grey, red and white hair respond poorly.
deepLead:
The Philips Lumea is a handheld consumer device for hair removal at home using intense pulsed light (IPL). It is one of several home IPL products sold as an alternative to treatment in a clinic.
IPL is not a laser: it uses a flashlamp emitting broad-spectrum light that is absorbed mainly by melanin in the hair follicle.  Encyclopedic sources describe IPL as generally less effective than laser hair removal, though many users are satisfied, and say it works best on darker, coarser hair. 
No sources reviewed for this article report trials of the Lumea specifically; the discussion below therefore concerns home IPL devices as a category.

name: Tria Beauty hair removal laser

angle.text: Users buy the Tria as an at-home diode laser for longer-lasting hair reduction than shaving provides. It is one of two over-the-counter diode lasers the FDA had cleared as of 2025, and the clearance covers hair reduction.

summary: An at-home diode laser for hair reduction, one of two over-the-counter diode devices the FDA had cleared as of 2025.
note: Dark, coarse hair on lighter skin responds best; light, grey, red and fine hair respond poorly.
currentQuick:
The Tria is a consumer diode laser for hair removal at home. According to Wikipedia, it is one of two diode devices the US FDA had cleared for over-the-counter sale as of 2025.
Laser hair removal in clinics is described as producing long-term hair reduction rather than total removal, usually needing several sessions. Sources specific to the Tria were limited, so this article is short.
How it works: Laser energy is absorbed by melanin in the hair and heats the follicle (selective photothermolysis), damaging it while sparing most surrounding skin. Treatments are repeated over weeks to months.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are redness, itching and swelling lasting a few days; burns, pigment changes and eye injury are possible. Results vary by hair and skin colour.
deepLead:
The Tria is a hair-removal diode laser sold for home use. Wikipedia states that, as of 2025, the US FDA had cleared two diode devices for over-the-counter sale, the Epilaser and the TRIA. 
Professional laser hair removal works by selective photothermolysis: light absorbed by melanin heats the hair follicle.  It is cleared for "permanent hair reduction", meaning a long-term decrease in regrowth rather than total removal.

name: Silk'n Infinity / Flash&Go

angle.text: Users apply Silk'n Infinity and Flash&Go devices at home for gradual hair reduction. A small early study of the brand's home pulsed-light device reported hair reduction; the specific current models are less studied.

summary: Silk'n home light-based hair-removal devices; an early small study of the brand's home pulsed light device reported hair reduction.
note: Study data are for an early Silk'n device, not necessarily these models.
currentQuick:
Silk'n makes home light-based hair-removal devices, including the Infinity and Flash&Go lines. They use low-energy pulsed light designed for self-treatment.
A 2009 study of an early Silk'n home pulsed light device tested 34 people and 92 sites with blinded hair counts. Sources on the Infinity and Flash&Go models themselves were not found.
How it works: Home pulsed light is absorbed by hair melanin, heating the follicle. Silk'n devices are described as small, light, low-energy and low-cost IPL systems.
Risks and caveats: A 2010 review of home IPL devices noted they are designed to cause biological damage to follicles, with eye safety a key design concern. Home-use IPL is generally considered less suited to very dark skin or light hair.
deepLead:
Silk'n is a brand of home light-based hair-removal devices, including the Infinity and Flash&Go models. An early device from the brand, made by HomeSkinovations of Israel, was described in a 2009 study as a small, light-weight, low-energy, low-cost IPL system for home use. 
The 2009 study tested the device on 34 people and 92 sites, with self-treatment supervised in clinic and hair counts done by a blinded observer.  The sources reviewed contain no trial specific to the Infinity or Flash&Go models.
